edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE
edition.deck: A cockpit attack, strikes on Kyiv’s bridges and high-stakes elections abroad lead a day of consequential news. At home, benefit reforms, a fuel squeeze and a pause in Danish citizenship decisions raise urgent questions.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and substantial reporting across international affairs, UK policy and Danish public life. Related coverage has been grouped where it adds evidence or a distinct dimension; allegations and unsettled questions remain attributed.

content.headline: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe during flight, UAE says
content.shortHeadline: UAE says Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe
content.standfirst: Passengers helped subdue the co-pilot after an Israel-bound plane plunged sharply; reserve pilots landed it safely in Saudi Arabia. Investigators have yet to establish the suspect’s motive or whether anyone else was involved.

image.caption: Captain Smit Machchhar, praised for his actions during the attack.

sources.originalTitle: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
Anklager: Andenpilot brugte økse under angreb i cockpit
Flydubai co-pilot used crash axe to attack captain, says UAE

segments.body: The UAE prosecutor general says the co-pilot attacked the captain with a crash axe and tried to take control of the Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The plane plunged about 17,000ft before passengers entered the cockpit and helped subdue him; two reserve pilots then landed in Saudi Arabia.

segments.title: Questions for investigators
segments.body: The UAE is leading the investigation, with other countries participating. The Guardian reports that investigators are examining how the co-pilot came to be flying for the airline after Oman Air removed him from flying over concerns about extremist views. The extent of his vetting at Flydubai is unclear.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s account highlights a key security question: Israel says it has agreements with foreign carriers about pilots from countries with which it has no diplomatic relations, including Oman. The investigation has not established how that issue applied here.

content.headline: Russian strikes hit Kyiv’s major bridges as residents fear worsening attacks
content.shortHeadline: Russian strikes hit Kyiv bridges as residents fear more attacks
content.standfirst: A strike damaged the Northern Bridge after repeated attacks on the Southern Bridge, disrupting key routes across the capital. Residents interviewed by DR describe anxiety about further strikes and a winter that could bring shortages of heat, power and water.

image.caption: Kyiv’s Northern Bridge, the second major bridge in the city reported hit in recent days.

sources.originalTitle: Russia strikes second major bridge in Kyiv, mayor says
Russiske droneangreb skaber frygt i Kyiv: Borgere overvejer at forlade byen

segments.body: Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko says a Russian strike damaged the road surface and trolleybus wires on the Northern Bridge, blocking traffic across the river. It followed repeated drone attacks on the Southern Bridge, which have disrupted metro and car travel. Russia said the Northern Bridge was used for troop transfers and logistics.

segments.title: Civilians face a difficult winter
segments.body: A journalist in Kyiv told DR that some residents are considering leaving as ordinary journeys feel more dangerous. Former Danish intelligence analyst Jacob Kaarsbo says Russia’s newer jet drones are difficult for Ukrainian air defences to intercept, while missile-defence supplies are inadequate. The scale of the risk to civilians remains uncertain.

perspectives.body: DR’s reporting conveys residents’ concerns beyond the immediate bridge damage: people fear losing heat, electricity and water over winter, and some are already considering leaving Kyiv. These are accounts of expectations, not confirmed forecasts of what will happen.

content.headline: French education protests spread as 1,747 people are arrested
content.shortHeadline: French school protests spread; 1,747 arrested
content.standfirst: Protests over staffing, crowded classrooms and school conditions have disrupted 735 schools, according to the education minister. The demonstrations have turned violent in places, while students and unions say their concerns about education remain unresolved.

image.caption: A fire burns in the street as protesters blockade a school in Brest.

sources.originalTitle: Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France

segments.body: Riot police clashed with protesters as demonstrations spread from Paris to cities including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 1,747 people were arrested on Friday; Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 735 of France’s 3,700 schools were affected. The education ministry says at least 65 staff members have been injured.

segments.title: Dispute over the protests
segments.body: Students cite staff shortages, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings, and several unions support the protests. Ministers say the movement has been hijacked by non-students; police point to seized weapons and damage to schools. A 17-year-old was arrested on suspicion of attempted homicide after a police officer was attacked in Belfort.

content.headline: G7 agrees release of 100 million barrels to ease fuel supply fears
content.shortHeadline: G7 to release 100 million barrels to ease fuel supply fears
content.standfirst: The coordinated release of oil and diesel is intended to ease pressure on supply and prices while avoiding a US export ban. It is a short-term intervention, and the countries’ stocks and the timing of some releases remain uncertain.

sources.originalTitle: G7 to release millions of barrels of oil and diesel after Trump threat
Three reasons Middle East oil supply is nearly back to pre-Iran war levels

segments.body: G7 leaders say a coordinated release of 100 million barrels of oil and diesel will begin immediately and run over four months, including a substantial diesel release within 20 days. The agreement also rules out energy export restrictions among G7 members, after President Donald Trump threatened a US diesel export ban.

segments.title: A buffer, not a settled market
segments.body: The reserves are intended to ease immediate supply concerns, but it is not yet clear which partner countries will contribute or how quickly. Kpler data reported by BBC Verify indicates Middle Eastern oil flows have recovered to 92% of their pre-war baseline, helped by pipelines, US support for shipping and tanker transfers. Analysts caution the arrangements remain vulnerable to further attacks or policy changes.

perspectives.body: BBC Verify’s analysis shows how much of the region’s oil has been rerouted around the Strait of Hormuz, but also the limits of that recovery: oil-product and liquefied natural gas flows remain well below pre-conflict levels, and shipping through the strait is still exposed to attack.

content.headline: Spain’s government loses housing vote after protests over eviction
content.shortHeadline: Spain’s government loses housing vote after eviction protests
content.standfirst: Parliament rejected two measures intended to protect tenants after a disputed eviction helped galvanise protests. The defeat exposes the minority government’s fragile position and adds to speculation about an early election.

image.caption: Pedro Sánchez appealed to lawmakers to support the housing measures before the votes.

sources.originalTitle: Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87
Boligkrisen har sendt spaniere på gaden - nu kan den føre til tidligt valg, vurderer korrespondent

segments.body: Spain’s Congress rejected two government decrees intended to address the housing crisis, by 178 votes to 172 and 184 to 166. The proposals included extending some rental contracts and suspending evictions of vulnerable tenants. The measures followed protests over the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid home.

segments.title: A political setback
segments.body: The defeat underlines that Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez does not command a parliamentary majority. The government was relying on smaller parties, but Together for Catalonia opposed the decrees, arguing they were hastily prepared and could have the opposite effect. Spanish media reported that the government would consider its next move over the weekend; an early election remains speculation.

perspectives.body: DR’s Europe correspondent Anna Gaarslev describes housing as a broad-based public movement in Spain, not simply a response to one eviction. She says Sánchez could use the parliamentary defeat to argue that voters should decide the direction of housing policy.

content.headline: Deadly Bangkok floods overwhelm the city as scientists warn of heavier rain
content.shortHeadline: Deadly floods overwhelm Bangkok as rainfall risks grow
content.standfirst: Around 40 people have died and all 50 districts have been declared a flood disaster area after exceptional rainfall overwhelmed drainage systems. Scientists say extreme rain is increasing in the region, while cautioning that these specific floods need further study.

sources.originalTitle: Bangkok at breaking point as floods turn streets into stagnant lakes

segments.body: About 300mm of rain fell in parts of Bangkok in roughly two days, turning neighbourhoods into stagnant lakes. The government says around 40 people died in flood-related incidents and thousands stayed in shelters. Flooding disrupted the airport, closed schools and left much of the capital gridlocked; authorities warn further rain is possible.

segments.title: Why the city struggled
segments.body: Bangkok’s canals, pumps and dikes could not cope with the rainfall, which in some places exceeded drainage capacity. Scientists say warming seas and air can intensify downpours, and research points to a longer-term increase in extreme rainfall in central Thailand. They caution it is too early to attribute these particular rains to climate change; a low-pressure system and a strong El Niño also shaped conditions.

content.headline: Brazil’s close election could reshape Latin America’s alignment with Trump
content.shortHeadline: Brazil election could reshape Latin America’s alignment with Trump
content.standfirst: Polls show a tight contest between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro. The result could alter regional alignments with Washington, though a runoff on 25 October is possible if neither candidate wins a majority.

image.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro supporters at a rally in São Paulo with an inflatable figure of Donald Trump.

sources.originalTitle: Brazil’s neck-and-neck election offers test for growing pro-Trump Latin American bloc
The knife-edge election Trump is watching as a blueprint for the midterms

segments.body: Brazil votes in a presidential race that polls suggest is close between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. If neither wins more than half the vote, a runoff is due on 25 October. Analysts see the election as a test of whether the region’s largest country will align more closely with US President Donald Trump.

segments.title: Foreign policy and democratic concerns
segments.body: The candidates differ on Trump’s regional security coalition, relations with China and access to Brazil’s critical minerals. Analysts warn a Bolsonaro victory could strengthen the far right and deepen US influence; others point to economic concerns, allegations under investigation and anti-Lula sentiment as factors in his support. The outcome remains unpredictable.

perspectives.body: The i’s correspondent argues that Trump’s support for Bolsonaro and pressure on Brazil have made the vote an unusually direct test of US influence. The column also stresses that the final outcome may depend on a runoff and the smaller parties’ voters.

content.headline: Latvia votes amid fears of Russian interference and pro-Russian gains
content.shortHeadline: Latvia votes amid fears of Russian interference and pro-Russian gains
content.standfirst: Latvian authorities say there is no concrete evidence of a planned attempt to disrupt the election, but cannot rule it out. Security fears are heightened by past drone incidents and polls suggesting a pro-Russian party could gain ground.

image.caption: Fighter jets and air-defence systems are helping secure Latvia’s airspace during the election.

sources.originalTitle: ANALYSE Det er ikke uden grund, at letterne vil holde ekstra øje med himlen, når de i dag skal til valg

segments.body: Latvia’s parliament election takes place amid concern about sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation linked to Russia. The country’s domestic security service says it has no concrete signs of a systematic effort to influence the result, but cannot rule out disruption. German fighter jets have been sent to help monitor the airspace.

segments.title: A contested political landscape
segments.body: Polls suggest the pro-Russian Sovereign Power party could become the second-largest, while the governing centre-right party is ahead. The analysis describes the parties’ differing positions on Russia and Ukraine, and the possibility that no one party can govern alone. The result is not known in the supplied reporting.

perspectives.body: DR’s analysis places the election in a wider security context: recent drone incidents have already affected Latvian politics, but officials have not said there is evidence of a specific plan to sabotage this vote.

content.headline: Poll finds 49% back rejoining EU as Labour weighs its next move
content.shortHeadline: Poll finds 49% back rejoining EU as Labour weighs its next move
content.standfirst: A survey of 11,461 people found rejoining the EU was the most popular of seven options tested, while other closer ties also drew support. Labour’s leaders remain divided over the political risks of reopening Brexit.

image.caption: A pro-EU campaigner calls for the UK to rejoin the bloc in Parliament Square.

sources.originalTitle: Half of UK wants to rejoin EU and backing it could drive up Labour vote, megapoll finds
How Farage plans to ‘set fire’ to a Burnham Brexit – and the plot to stop him

segments.body: A Messina Group poll found 49% supported rejoining the EU and 28.5% opposed it. Cutting trade barriers within the existing relationship was supported by 48.2%. The poll also found more than half thought Brexit had been a failure, but arguments about sovereignty and immigration still resonated.

segments.title: Political risks and choices
segments.body: Andy Burnham has called for a review of Britain’s options, including rejoining, but ministers and MPs remain wary of reviving Brexit divisions. The survey found support for a fresh referendum varied: almost a third wanted one first, while others thought an election mandate or Parliament could decide. Polling does not establish how voters would behave in an election.

perspectives.body: The i examines why electoral reform could be linked to closer EU ties: analysts say Brussels may be reluctant to negotiate a complex agreement if a future government could quickly reverse it. Proportional representation would not guarantee a pro-European majority.

content.headline: London council warns council tax could rise by 150% under funding cuts
content.shortHeadline: London council warns council tax could rise by 150%
content.standfirst: Hammersmith and Fulham says a 150% rise in its council tax element could be needed to balance its budget in 2027–28. The council blames a sharp reduction in central government funding; ministers say local authorities must put taxpayers first.

image.caption: Angela Rayner introduced the funding rules that Hammersmith and Fulham says will cut its grant.

sources.originalTitle: London Labour council warns it may raise council tax by 150%

segments.body: Hammersmith and Fulham council says its government grant will fall from £150.5m in 2025–26 to £72.4m over the next four years. Its report sets out a range of possible increases; a 150% rise in the council’s own tax element would add £29.11 a week for a Band D household and broadly balance its budget on current assumptions.

segments.title: Dispute over the funding formula
segments.body: The council says the government’s funding review penalises boroughs that have kept council tax low, despite deprivation in parts of the borough. Ministers say the changes are intended to direct more money to places with greater need and have made £78bn available for local government next year. The proposed increase is not a final decision.

content.headline: UK regulators urged to scrutinise bets on whether HSBC and Lloyds will fail
content.shortHeadline: UK regulators urged to scrutinise bets on bank failures
content.standfirst: Polymarket has offered bets on whether major banks, including HSBC and Lloyds, will fail by year-end. Critics warn that prediction markets could amplify panic or invite manipulation; the company argues they widen access to information.

sources.originalTitle: UK urged to act as Polymarket takes bets on whether HSBC and Lloyds will fail

segments.body: The Guardian reports that users have taken $77,507 in positions on whether major banks will fail, including HSBC and Lloyds. UK residents are barred from the platform’s offshore service, but the Financial Conduct Authority says it has discussed prediction markets with international regulators as part of its work on market integrity.

segments.title: Risk of speculation spreading
segments.body: A Treasury committee member says regulators should contact their US counterparts, warning that a rapidly growing market could affect sentiment and potentially contribute to a bank run. European securities regulators have separately warned of insider-trading and manipulation risks. Polymarket says the markets make information more accessible; the banks declined to comment.

content.headline: BT temporarily paused broadband for customers who had not switched landlines
content.shortHeadline: BT paused broadband for some customers over landline switch
content.standfirst: BT says a small group of customers who had ignored years of notices received five days’ warning before a temporary broadband pause. Campaigners fear the wider move to digital landlines could leave vulnerable people without reliable access to help.

image.caption: About 1.3 million copper-based landlines are still to be migrated to digital services.

sources.originalTitle: BT accused of ‘bullying’ customers by pausing broadband in digital landline push

segments.body: About 1.3 million copper landlines remain to be migrated before the planned end-of-January retirement of the old network. BT says it temporarily paused broadband for a small group of customers who had not responded to communications for two years; more than 80% then took steps to switch. Landline and mobile services remained available during the pauses.

segments.title: Concern over vulnerable households
segments.body: Campaigners say some remaining customers are older, live in areas with patchy mobile coverage or rely on telecare. The industry deadline was delayed after earlier migrations left some older and disabled people without working alarms. For most customers, BT says the change involves plugging a phone into a broadband router rather than a wall socket.

content.headline: Labour faces rebellion risks over welfare reforms and pension triple lock
content.shortHeadline: Labour faces rebellion risks over welfare and pension reforms
content.standfirst: Reviews are expected to shape changes to disability benefits and support for young people, while Andy Burnham’s pension proposals have unsettled MPs. The government says any move from cash to services for PIP claimants would be voluntary.

image.caption: Imali Chislett, a 25-year-old PIP claimant from Southampton.

sources.originalTitle: The Labour mutiny Burnham faces over triple lock and welfare reforms
I’m a PIP claimant – here’s how I spend my £780 payment

segments.body: The government is awaiting the Timms review of personal independence payments and the Milburn review of young people out of work, education or training. One proposal under discussion is allowing some claimants to choose services or equipment instead of cash. Disability minister Stephen Timms has said this would be voluntary; the reviews’ recommendations are not yet published.

segments.title: Claimants and MPs question the detail
segments.body: PIP claimant Imali Chislett says cash gives her flexibility to meet disability-related costs, including transport, energy and adapted mobility needs. Disability groups warn that replacing cash could worsen wellbeing and poverty. Labour MPs also caution that cuts or sanctions should not precede meaningful support into work; the scope of any reforms remains undecided.

perspectives.body: Chislett’s account gives a concrete picture of costs PIP helps meet: her mobility payment goes towards a Motability car, while parking, taxis, energy and wheelchair parts add further expenses. She worries that promised services may not be available when needed.

content.headline: UK hauliers urge fuel duty relief as diesel hits record £2 a litre
content.shortHeadline: Hauliers seek fuel duty relief as diesel tops £2 a litre
content.standfirst: G7 plans to release emergency stocks have not eased warnings that high diesel costs could feed into food prices and squeeze transport firms. The government says drivers still benefit from a temporary fuel-duty cut and says there will be no rise this year.

image.caption: A petrol station in Bristol as UK diesel prices reach a record high.

sources.originalTitle: Truckers plea for fuel duty bailout as diesel prices hit record high

segments.body: The RAC says the average price of diesel reached 200.01p a litre, a record, while petrol averaged 174.71p. The Road Haulage Association says hauliers typically pay £350 more a week to fill an HGV than in February and is calling for a pause to planned duty increases and a rebate for essential users.

segments.title: Relief may be temporary
segments.body: An energy expert says releasing reserves can ease immediate pressure but reduces the buffer against future disruption and does not resolve dependence on international markets. The government says its extension of the 5p fuel-duty cut leaves diesel 11p a litre cheaper than under the previous government’s plans until year-end.

content.headline: EU drops opposition to transition periods in UK food-trade talks
content.shortHeadline: EU drops opposition to transition periods in food-trade talks
content.standfirst: Negotiators are discussing extra time for UK businesses to adapt if Britain aligns with EU rules on animal and plant health. The talks are part of a possible package of agreements, but the separate dispute over youth mobility remains unresolved.

image.caption: UK and EU negotiators are seeking agreement on food trade and other post-Brexit issues.

sources.originalTitle: Brexit deal inches closer as EU gives ground to UK on food and drink

segments.body: The EU has dropped its opposition to transition periods in negotiations over a UK-EU food and drink agreement. British businesses have warned that an immediate switch to EU animal, plant and health rules could cost hundreds of millions of pounds. The two sides are aiming to reach agreement on food trade, youth mobility and carbon markets.

segments.title: Other disagreements remain
segments.body: The UK and EU are still apart over youth-mobility visa numbers and whether European students would pay lower tuition fees at British universities. The UK has proposed a cap of 50,000 visas, while the EU has asked for 150,000. The timing and terms of any final agreements have not been settled.

content.headline: Plan to reduce armed guards on some nuclear waste shipments raises safety debate
content.shortHeadline: Plan to cut guards on some nuclear shipments raises safety debate
content.standfirst: The Nuclear Decommissioning Authority says security could be tailored to risk, saving money without compromising safety. Critics warn that reducing armed escorts for sensitive material needs clear safeguards amid warnings about hostile-state activity.

image.caption: Special trains transport nuclear material around the UK; the most dangerous loads are escorted.

sources.originalTitle: Nuclear waste armed guards face cuts under cost-saving plan

segments.body: The Nuclear Decommissioning Authority is proposing that armed escorts could be removed from some nuclear waste shipments where they do not provide a proportionate security benefit. The proposal covers material including plutonium and enriched uranium. Industry leaders say changes could cut some transport costs by 10% to 20%.

segments.title: Security and public confidence
segments.body: A former Civil Nuclear Constabulary officer argues the material needs a strong deterrent force. A Royal United Services Institute expert says cutting escorts would not necessarily increase risk, but the government must explain which loads would be excluded and how security will be maintained. The NDA and police say any changes would be made with regulators and must not compromise safety.

content.headline: Danmark sætter statsborgerskab på pause – også statsløse børn venter
content.shortHeadline: Pause i statsborgerskab efterlader ansøgere og børn i uvished
content.standfirst: Folketinget har ikke godkendt nye statsborgere siden juni 2025, og sager afventer en undersøgelse af screening for antidemokratiske holdninger. Eksperter advarer om mulige konventionsbrud for statsløse børn født i Danmark.

image.caption: Saeid Ashian og hans kone Mia, mens familiens statsborgerskabssager er sat på pause.

sources.originalTitle: Saeid var næsten dansk statsborger. Nu er familien så utryg, at de overvejer at forlade Danmark
Eksperter: Danmark bryder konventioner, hvis 231 bestemte børn ikke får statsborgerskab

segments.body: I januar var 2.055 personer indstillet til at blive danske statsborgere, men lovforslaget faldt efter valget, og behandlingen er sat på pause. DR oplyser, at 72 statsløse børn født i Danmark dengang opfyldte kravene. I alt kan 231 statsløse børn være berørt, mens mange sager endnu ikke er behandlet.

segments.title: Eksperter rejser rettighedsspørgsmål
segments.body: Seniorforsker Eva Ersbøll mener, at en langvarig pause kan stride mod Danmarks forpligtelse til at undgå statsløshed. Advokat Jytte Lindgård siger, at genbehandling efter nye regler også kan krænke børns rettigheder. Det afhænger blandt andet af, hvor længe sagerne står stille, og om de åbnes igen til efteråret.

perspectives.body: Saeid Ashian, som opfyldte kravene og var indstillet i januar, fortæller DR, at familien nu er usikker på, om den skal forlade Danmark. Hans kone og børn er heller ikke danske statsborgere; familien siger, at den helst vil blive.

content.headline: Tre teenagere tiltalt for drabsforsøg efter 15 skud mod lejlighed i Kastrup
content.shortHeadline: Tre teenagere tiltalt efter 15 skud mod lejlighed i Kastrup
content.standfirst: Anklagemyndigheden mener, at de dengang 17, 17 og 18 år gamle drenge blev hyret til et drabsforsøg. En familie, herunder børn, var i lejligheden, men ingen kom til skade; to af de tiltalte nægter sig skyldige.

image.caption: En familie med børn var i lejligheden, da der blev skudt mod den; ingen blev ramt.

sources.originalTitle: Teenagere tiltalt for drabsforsøg efter skud mod lejlighed i Kastrup

segments.body: Tre teenagedrenge er tiltalt for drabsforsøg efter, at der i marts blev affyret 15 skud mod en families lejlighed i Kastrup. Ifølge anklageskriftet blev våbnet overdraget i en Ikea-pose, og drengene ventede på instruktioner fra en ukendt medgerningsmand. Ingen i lejligheden kom til skade.

segments.title: En sag om bestilt vold
segments.body: Politiet beskriver lignende sager som “violence as a service”, hvor unge hyres til kriminalitet; i denne sag er de tiltalte danske teenagere. To af drengene nægter sig skyldige, og det er uvist, hvordan den tredje forholder sig til tiltalen.

content.headline: Ny app samler kvinders beretninger om overgreb – ekspert advarer mod frygt
content.shortHeadline: Overgrebsapp kan skabe utryghed, advarer ekspert
content.standfirst: Appen Beloud.now markerer brugeres beretninger om chikane, stalking og overgreb på et kort. En ekspert siger, at prikkerne kan give et misvisende indtryk af risikoen; anonyme opslag kan også være falske.

image.caption: Lærke Schou bruger appen til at dele en oplevelse og se andre brugeres markeringer.

sources.originalTitle: Kvinder advarer hinanden om overgreb og chikane i ny app: Men ekspert advarer imod den

segments.body: Beloud.now er kommet til Danmark, og appen viser over 2.000 markeringer baseret på brugeres beretninger om blandt andet overgreb, stalking og drugging. Brugeren Lærke Schou fortæller, at hun kan vælge en anden rute, hvis et område har flere markeringer om vold eller drugging.

segments.title: Synlighed mod risiko for misbrug
segments.body: Det Kriminalpræventive Råds Tine Fuglsang advarer om, at kortet kan få risikoen til at virke større, end den er, og understreger, at nattelivet for de fleste unge er trygt. Appens udvikler siger, at formålet er at synliggøre hændelser, der ikke anmeldes, men anerkender, at appen kan misbruges. Københavns Politi opfordrer til anmeldelser.

content.headline: Forskning: Grænsehandel koster staten mindre end hidtil beregnet
content.shortHeadline: Grænsehandel koster staten mindre end hidtil anslået
content.standfirst: Et studie af danskernes forbrug under coronanedlukningen anslår statens tab på grænsehandel med nydelsesmidler til 415 millioner kroner i 2019 – mod Skatteministeriets hypotetiske beregning på 1,16 milliarder. Forskerne siger, at forbrug ikke flytter én til én til danske butikker.

image.caption: Grænsen til Tyskland var midlertidigt lukket under coronanedlukningen.

sources.originalTitle: Staten taber ikke så mange penge på grænsehandel, som vi hidtil har troet, viser ny forskning

segments.body: Forskere fra Københavns Universitet brugte den midlertidige lukning af grænsen under coronapandemien til at undersøge danskernes forbrug. De vurderer, at statens tab på grænsehandel med blandt andet slik, chips, øl og sodavand var 415 millioner kroner i 2019, når tobak ikke medregnes.

segments.title: Effekten var lokal
segments.body: Forbruget af danske nydelsesmidler steg 109 procent blandt personer, der boede højst 30 kilometer fra grænsen, da grænsebutikkerne blev utilgængelige. Effekten blev mindre og forsvandt ved længere afstande; forskerne fandt ingen tilsvarende ændring for grænsehandel til Sverige. Skatteministeriet havde ikke nået at kommentere studiet.

content.headline: Kujalleq stopper midlertidigt salg og udskænkning af alkohol
content.shortHeadline: Kommune i Grønland stopper alkoholsalg midlertidigt
content.standfirst: Kujalleqs borgmester bad Naalakkersuisut standse salg og udskænkning for at beskytte børn og befolkningens sikkerhed. Regeringen har efterkommet anmodningen, men det er uklart, hvor længe forbuddet skal gælde.

image.caption: Narsaq ligger i Kujalleq Kommune i det sydlige Grønland.

sources.originalTitle: Grønlandsk kommune stopper salg af alkohol

segments.body: Salg og udskænkning af alkohol i Kujalleq i Sydgrønland blev stoppet fredag, efter at borgmester Malene Wahl Rasmussen bad den grønlandske regering gribe ind. Naalakkersuisut siger, at formålet med den midlertidige lukning er at beskytte børns tarv og befolkningens sikkerhed.

segments.title: Ingen slutdato meldt ud
segments.body: Det er endnu uklart, hvor længe forbuddet gælder. DR bemærker, at der også under coronapandemien blev indført et midlertidigt forbud mod udskænkning af stærkere alkohol i Nuuk, Kapisillit og Qeqertarsuatsiaat, dengang med henvisning til beskyttelse af børn, der var hjemme.

content.headline: Politiet undersøger mulig sammenhæng mellem overfald ved Risskov
content.shortHeadline: Politiet undersøger, om overfald ved Risskov hænger sammen
content.standfirst: To unge kvinder er blevet overfaldet i Risskov med godt to måneders mellemrum, og politiet undersøger, om sagerne hænger sammen. Beboere vil gå ture i området, men politiet fraråder private vagtværn og siger, at ekstra patruljer sættes ind.

image.caption: Politiet siger, at det endnu er for tidligt at afgøre, om overfaldene hænger sammen.

sources.originalTitle: Politiet efterforsker, om overfald på unge kvinder ved Risskov kan hænge sammen
Overfald på kvindelige løbere får Jacob til at samle bekymrede naboer til aftenture i skoven

segments.body: Østjyllands Politi undersøger, om overfaldene på to kvinder i Risskov kan hænge sammen, men siger, at det er for tidligt at konkludere. Den seneste kvinde blev skubbet omkuld og holdt nede, men slap fri. Politiet har også talt med en kvinde, der følte sig forfulgt på Trøjborg.

segments.title: Beboere vil være synlige
segments.body: En gruppe lokale fædre har foreslået aftenture i små grupper efter overfaldene. Initiativtager Jacob Hou siger, at de ikke vil fungere som vagtværn, men gribe ind, hvis de ser et overfald. Politiet fraråder private patruljer, varsler ekstra synlig tilstedeværelse og beder vidner kontakte politiet.

perspectives.body: DR taler med initiativtager Jacob Hou, som siger, at gruppen vil være til stede og hjælpe, hvis nogen bliver overfaldet. Han afviser, at de vil antaste folk, men siger, at de vil tilbageholde en gerningsperson, hvis nødvendigt.

content.headline: Musikfolk advarer mod politisk pres på festivalers program
content.shortHeadline: Musikbranche advarer mod politisk indblanding i festivalprogrammer
content.standfirst: Branchefolk frygter, at trusler om at fjerne kommunal støtte får festivaler og spillesteder til at undgå kontroversielle kunstnere. Kommunalpolitikere må have holdninger, siger KL’s kulturudvalgsformand, men armslængdeprincippet skal respekteres.

image.caption: Musikeren Isam B, hvis booking har været omstridt i den lokale støtte-debat.

sources.originalTitle: 'Det er jo noget, vi ser i autoritære regimer': Musikbranche bekymret for politisk indblanding

segments.body: Musik over Præstø Fjord har mistet Næstved Kommunes tilskud til næste års program efter kontrovers om bookingen af Isam B; ikke alle i kommunen mener dog, at der er en sammenhæng. Sagen følger tidligere politisk pres mod spillestedet Vega og kritik af en optræden på Roskilde Festival.

segments.title: Frygt for selvcensur
segments.body: Dansk Live-direktør Esben Marcher advarer om, at økonomisk pres kan få især mindre kulturinstitutioner til at rette ind. En undersøgelse fra Dansk Kulturliv fandt, at 45% af lederne i 224 adspurgte kulturinstitutioner og virksomheder oplevede politisk pres i nogen eller høj grad. KL’s Lone Loklindt siger, at armslængdeprincippet skal respekteres.

content.headline: Olivia Dean anklages for at have lånt musikalske træk fra Bill Withers-hit
content.shortHeadline: Olivia Dean møder anklage om lighed med Bill Withers-hit
content.standfirst: En rettighedsforvalter for Bill Withers’ sangkatalog mener, at Olivia Deans “I’ve Seen It” gentagne gange låner fra “Just The Two of Us”. Søgsmålet retter sig mod pladeselskabet og musikforlagene, ikke mod Dean eller hendes medforfattere personligt.

image.caption: Olivia Dean med sin Grammy for bedste nye kunstner.

sources.originalTitle: Kan du høre ligheden? Olivia Dean-hit anklages for at låne for meget fra soulklassiker

segments.body: Mattie Music Group siger, at melodierne i “I’ve Seen It” og Bill Withers’ “Just The Two of Us” deler markante musikalske træk. Søgsmålet nævner Olivia Deans pladeselskab Capitol Records, Universal Music Group og sangerens musikforlag; der kræves ikke erstatning fra Dean selv eller hendes medforfattere.

segments.title: Påstandene er ikke afgjort
segments.body: “I’ve Seen It” udkom på Deans album The Art of Loving i september 2025. DR opfordrer lyttere til selv at sammenligne sangene, men det fremlagte materiale indeholder ikke en afgørelse eller en kommentar fra Deans pladeselskab.

content.headline: Venom’s Cronos made metal raw, dangerous and impossible to ignore
content.shortHeadline: How Venom’s Cronos made metal raw and dangerous
content.standfirst: Conrad “Cronos” Lant, who has died aged 63, helped turn Venom’s DIY ferocity and occult theatrics into a blueprint for black metal and an influence on generations of heavy bands.

image.caption: Cronos performing in 1985.

sources.originalTitle: No one could terrify like Cronos, the black metal innovator who reignited rock’s hellraising attitude
Conrad ‘Cronos’ Lant, frontman of UK heavy metal band Venom, dies aged 63

segments.title: A new kind of menace
segments.body: When Venom emerged from Newcastle in the late 1970s, Lant thought metal had gone soft. The band brought punk’s unruly spirit to heavier music: hammering riffs, hoarse vocals and lyrics that made occult imagery confrontational. The hostility from critics only sharpened the group’s appeal.

segments.title: Influence without endorsement
segments.body: Venom’s 1982 album Black Metal gave a name to a subgenre, while the band’s raw sound helped shape thrash acts including Metallica, Slayer and Anthrax. Lant did not endorse the violence associated with parts of the later Norwegian scene; he said it was a shame its members were known for violence rather than music.

perspectives.body: Venom’s statement described Lant’s voice, bass and vision as central to the band for more than four decades, saying he helped create music that changed heavy music for ever. It gave no cause of death.

content.headline: Grouper’s Liz Harris finds connection in Helen, and wariness in streaming
content.shortHeadline: Grouper’s Liz Harris on collaboration and streaming scams
content.standfirst: A viral resurgence brought new listeners to Liz Harris’s music—and a fraudster trying to claim royalties. Reforming dream-pop trio Helen, meanwhile, has reminded the famously independent artist of the restorative power of making music together.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Grouper and Helen.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.title: A different kind of music-making
segments.body: Harris describes Grouper as intensely solitary, but says she can relax more in Helen, her trio with Jed Bindeman and Scott Simmons. The band’s new album, Linda’s Head, has a brighter, more collective energy. Practising with friends helped lift her spirits while she was navigating medical difficulties.

segments.title: The cost of going viral
segments.body: When Grouper’s 2008 song Poison Tree found a new audience on TikTok, Harris learned that someone else had fraudulently uploaded and registered it. She and her label were able to shut down the scam and recover what she was owed. Fake remixes and tracks with her titles remain a concern, she says, and have reinforced her fear of entering the music industry more deeply.

content.headline: Erasure’s Andy Bell and Vince Clarke carry each other through grief
content.shortHeadline: Erasure’s 40-year friendship, grief and a changed tour
content.standfirst: As Erasure prepare their 20th album, Bell and Clarke talk about the friendship that helped them through bereavement. Clarke will direct their coming tour remotely after the death of his wife.

image.caption: Vince Clarke and Andy Bell.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s a deep soul connection’: Erasure on how 40 years of friendship got them through grief – and why Vince Clarke has quit touring

segments.title: A friendship tested by loss
segments.body: Clarke says Bell gave him the love and support he needed after his wife, Tracy Hurley Martin, died of cancer in 2024. Bell, who lost his partner Paul Hickey in 2012, says the pair have had to hold each other up. They describe a bond deeper than friendship, built over the four decades since Erasure formed.

segments.title: A new shape for the tour
segments.body: Radio!! Radio!! is Erasure’s 20th album, but its UK and European arena tour will be the first without Clarke on stage. He will serve as musical director remotely, with keyboard technician Howard Rider playing the synths. Bell admits it will not feel the same, even as he reassures Clarke that the crew will be with him.

content.headline: Bill Withers’ estate sues over alleged similarities in Olivia Dean song
content.shortHeadline: Olivia Dean faces a copyright lawsuit over “I’ve Seen It”
content.standfirst: Mattie Music Group alleges that Dean’s “I’ve Seen It” copied protectable musical elements from Bill Withers and Grover Washington Jr’s “Just the Two of Us”. The singer and her collaborators are not named as defendants.

image.caption: Olivia Dean performing at the 2026 BRIT Awards.

sources.originalTitle: Olivia Dean accused of plagiarism on her I’ve Seen It track

segments.title: What the lawsuit alleges
segments.body: The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Los Angeles, names Dean’s publisher and record label, along with a publisher for collaborator Max Wolfgang. It alleges that “I’ve Seen It”, the closing track on Dean’s 2025 album The Art of Loving, copied substantial aspects of the 1981 song, including its melody. The allegations have not been established in court.

segments.title: An analysis cited by the plaintiff
segments.body: Mattie Music Group says it hired musicologist Alexander Stewart, who concluded that the songs share substantial similarities in protectable musical expression. The lawsuit seeks damages and an injunction. The Guardian reported that representatives for Dean, Capitol Records and Kobalt had not immediately responded to its requests for comment; Kobalt declined to comment to Billboard.

content.headline: Marc Almond says Soft Cell’s final album became a farewell to Dave Ball
content.shortHeadline: Marc Almond on Soft Cell’s final album and Dave Ball
content.standfirst: Soft Cell had finished Danceteria together when keyboardist Dave Ball died two days later. Marc Almond says he would not make another album under the band’s name without him.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.title: A record they completed together
segments.body: Almond and Ball agreed that Danceteria was finished in October 2025, two days before Ball died aged 66. Almond calls it Soft Cell’s sixth and final album: he says he would never make another without his longtime collaborator. Its songs look back to the pair’s early-1980s New York life and the club that gives the record its title.

segments.title: A scene’s exuberance and loss
segments.body: Almond recalls New York’s underground clubs as a creative, dangerous world, but also remembers the fear and desolation as AIDS devastated the gay scene. He says the two were closer while making Danceteria than they had been for some time, and feels relieved they completed it together, even as he mourns that Ball will not see its release.

content.headline: This week’s new tracks: Heavensouls makes beautiful sense of breakneck chaos
content.shortHeadline: Heavensouls turns breakneck chaos into a new kind of beauty
content.standfirst: On Cantu of the Sower, Chidi Obialo turns noisy, high-speed contrasts into a vivid musical world. This week’s playlist also takes in new songs from Mei Semones, Angèle, Romy Mars and others.

image.caption: Chidi Obialo, who makes music as Heavensouls.

sources.originalTitle: Add to playlist: the beautiful, breakneck chaos of Heavensouls and the week’s best new tracks

segments.title: A listening guide
segments.body: The six songs on Heavensouls’ forthcoming Cantu of the Sower move between arcade-like glitter, crunching bass, playful breakbeats and warm brass. The review hears more than stylistic restlessness: found-sound snippets and a Stokely Carmichael sample help give the Nigerian-American artist’s abundance a sense of wonder and human connection.

segments.title: More new music to explore
segments.body: The selection ranges from Mei Semones’s bossa nova and strings on “Howl” to Angèle’s electroclash collaboration with Caroline Polachek and SebastiAn. It also highlights Madra Salach’s gothic folk, Blackhaine’s slow-building announcement of a debut album, and tracks from Romy Mars, Ryley Walker and Hodge.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s early years come into focus on an expansive reissue
content.shortHeadline: A 104-track Elvis Costello set traces the making of My Aim Is True
content.standfirst: A 104-track anniversary box set follows the restless songwriting behind Costello’s debut, from earlier demos to the Attractions taking shape. The review finds the wealth of material illuminating, if not every disc equally essential.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.title: A debut with a history
segments.body: The review argues that My Aim Is True was less a bolt from the blue than the culmination of a young songwriter’s experiments. Early recordings with Flip City show Costello working through rootsy influences before the sharp-edged persona of the debut came into focus. The set’s demos and live material make that gradual transformation newly audible.

segments.title: A deluxe set with uneven discoveries
segments.body: The box includes early demos, performances with the band Clover and recordings of the Attractions finding their footing. The reviewer finds the second disc, The Blue Print, especially revealing; later live material is enjoyable but less essential. Together, the five discs place the debut in the context of a remarkable run to come.

content.headline: Hayley Kiyoko turns “Girls Like Girls” into a love letter to her younger self
content.shortHeadline: Hayley Kiyoko on making “Girls Like Girls” a queer love story
content.standfirst: The singer has directed a feature based on her 2015 breakthrough song, drawing on teenage heartbreak and the representation she missed growing up. She calls releasing it in the current climate a chance to affirm queer love and joy.

image.caption: Hayley Kiyoko.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s radical to release a film called Girls Like Girls in this climate’: hitmaker turned director Hayley Kiyoko on sexuality, safety and becoming ‘Lesbian Jesus’

segments.title: A story that took a decade to reach the screen
segments.body: Kiyoko says “Girls Like Girls” was the subject she was most afraid to write about, and that the response to the song and video helped her feel more confident in her sexuality. After a YA novel helped the project get greenlit, she adapted the story into a feature she describes as a love letter to her 16- and 17-year-old self.

segments.title: Representation and queer joy
segments.body: Kiyoko wanted the film’s queer romance to reflect her Asian heritage, too. She says she rarely saw her experience as a queer, mixed-race Asian person reflected in cinemas while growing up. Though the characters face adversity, Kiyoko chose an intentionally positive portrayal, saying it matters to show queer people thriving in a hostile political climate.

content.headline: Digger divides critics over Tom Cruise’s oil-tycoon eco-satire
content.shortHeadline: Tom Cruise’s Digger splits critics on its eco-satire and performance
content.standfirst: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s film casts Cruise as a blustering oil baron facing a climate catastrophe. Reviews range from a damning verdict on its laborious storytelling to praise for its audacious scale and political bite.

image.caption: Tom Cruise as oil tycoon Digger Rockwell in Digger.

sources.originalTitle: Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire
Digger review: Tom Cruise takes the 'biggest risk of his career' in this 'love-it-or-hate-it' folly ★★★★☆
Tom Cruise has forgotten how to act

segments.title: A climate crisis—and a film that won’t stay in one lane
segments.body: Digger’s oil-drilling disaster brings its tycoon into a White House crisis meeting, where he challenges the politicians who depend on the industry he represents. The Guardian review finds the film shallow and laborious, arguing that its shifting tone and late narrative turn undercut the drama. The BBC review, by contrast, sees a politically blunt satire whose scenario feels uncomfortably plausible.

segments.title: Cruise’s performance is part of the argument
segments.body: Cruise plays Digger with prosthetics, a paunch and a pronounced Texan swagger. The i Paper review argues the star’s self-conscious effort to demonstrate his range overwhelms the character; the BBC calls the transformation a risky, eccentric choice and finds the scale of Cruise’s performance hard not to enjoy. The disagreements extend to the film’s excesses and its high-concept turns.

perspectives.body: The BBC reviewer argues that Digger’s political bluntness and unusual structure make it a love-it-or-hate-it folly rather than an obvious attempt to secure Cruise awards attention. Despite finding some excesses too long, the reviewer says the film’s ambition is part of its appeal.

content.headline: Paul Thomas Anderson captures Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall performance
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall is a concert film made to last
content.standfirst: Paul Thomas Anderson’s 35mm film preserves the Geese frontman’s stark solo performance and the hush of a rapt audience. The Guardian reviewer calls it an immediate classic, while noting it offers little for viewers who are not already drawn to Winter’s music.

image.caption: A still from Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall.

sources.originalTitle: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall review – Paul Thomas Anderson’s sumptuous recording is an immediate classic

segments.title: A concert, closely observed
segments.body: Shot over a 75-minute performance, the film keeps its focus on Winter at the piano, his singular voice and the audience’s attention. Anderson and his fellow camera operators largely stay out of the way; the film’s shifting light and close framing make the performance feel both intimate and expansive.

segments.title: A document for the already curious
segments.body: The reviewer says some of the show’s most communal moments do not translate fully to film, but that its quiet and the audience’s concentration do. With no interviews or narration to introduce Winter to newcomers, the film is aimed primarily at viewers already receptive to his music.

content.headline: Brassed Off at 30: Mark Herman says its story of a downtrodden town still speaks
content.shortHeadline: Brassed Off turns 30, and its politics still resonate
content.standfirst: Writer-director Mark Herman reflects on the unlikely success of his film about a South Yorkshire colliery band and the mining community around it. He says the mid-budget British films he wants to make are now difficult to get off the ground.

image.caption: Pete Postlethwaite in Brassed Off.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I thought Brassed Off might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley’: the director of Andy Burnham’s favourite film on its 30 year anniversary

segments.title: Comedy, music and political anger
segments.body: Brassed Off follows the Grimley Colliery Band as its members wait to learn whether their pit will close. Herman says audiences looking for comedy also found the film’s political message, while those expecting politics got comedy in return. He thinks its durability comes from a universal story about people being downtrodden.

segments.title: A film industry with less room for risk
segments.body: For the 30th anniversary, the band that inspired the film will perform its music alongside a screening at the Royal Albert Hall. Herman is pleased the film still reaches younger viewers, but says he has spent years trying to develop similar projects without success. He sees the current British market as divided between blockbusters and micro-budget films, leaving little room for mid-budget work.

content.headline: Bassam Tariq turns a stalled Blade project into a personal thriller
content.shortHeadline: Bassam Tariq salvages Blade plans for a new Mahershala Ali thriller
content.standfirst: In Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, Mahershala Ali plays a devout Muslim and contract killer trying to raise three children. Director Bassam Tariq says fight work developed for the abandoned Blade reboot found a new home in this more personal film.

image.caption: Bassam Tariq at the Toronto Film Festival in September 2026.

sources.originalTitle: How Bassam Tariq pivoted from stalled Blade reboot to new Mahershala Ali thriller: ‘I’m happier I made this movie’

segments.title: Faith, violence and fatherhood
segments.body: Tariq describes the Houston-set film as a pulpy thriller and a portrait of the city’s competing communities. Ali’s character, Latif, sees his violence as divine retribution, while trying to find his way back to his children. Tariq says the story’s attention to faith and fatherhood grew from conversations with Ali and from his own experience as a new parent.

segments.title: From Marvel preparation to an independent story
segments.body: Tariq says he and Ali had spent a year and a half preparing action sequences for Blade before he left the project in 2022. The reboot had no script, he says, and Marvel is not moving forward with it. They carried some of that fight choreography into this film; Tariq says he is happier making a project where he has room to explore his own ideas.

content.headline: A new Skywalker trilogy would keep Star Wars stuck in its family saga
content.shortHeadline: Star Wars should move beyond the Skywalker family
content.standfirst: A reported new trilogy has not been greenlit, and details remain scarce, but the possibility prompts a case for letting the franchise’s most famous family rest. The Guardian argues that its most intriguing stories have often looked elsewhere.

image.caption: Daisy Ridley as Rey in The Rise of Skywalker.

sources.originalTitle: A new Skywalker trilogy for Star Wars? Going back to the same family-saga well is a waste of time

segments.title: A report, not a green light
segments.body: The Guardian reports that Lucasfilm has hired Jon Watts to direct a possible new trilogy written by Simon Kinberg, with Daisy Ridley reportedly being considered for a return as Rey. The films have not been greenlit, and few details are known. The piece questions whether extending the Skywalker saga would offer anything beyond another return to familiar characters.

segments.title: The case for new corners of the galaxy
segments.body: The article argues that the Skywalker story has already been concluded more than once, and that Star Wars has found room to surprise when it steps outside the family drama. It points to Rogue One and Andor as examples, while acknowledging the pull of familiar characters—and the difficulty of persuading audiences that a story can end.

content.headline: Why horror films are pushed into the Golden Globes’ comedy category
content.shortHeadline: The Golden Globes leave horror with an awkward category choice
content.standfirst: Obsession is a violent horror story, yet its awards campaign is entering the musical or comedy categories. The rigid split between drama and comedy, the Guardian argues, leaves horror struggling for recognition either way.

image.caption: A still from Obsession.

sources.originalTitle: Horror films like Obsession are shut out of the Golden Globes – unless they pretend to be comedies

segments.title: A square peg in the awards ballot
segments.body: Focus Features plans to submit Obsession in the Golden Globes’ musical or comedy categories, despite its story of a man using a magical trinket to make a woman love him, with devastating results. The review argues that horror is often a poor fit for both major categories and can be pushed toward comedy simply because drama is more competitive.

segments.title: The stakes of category placement
segments.body: The piece notes that horror films have sometimes won recognition in comedy categories, as Demi Moore did for The Substance, even if that route may cost a film a shot at the top prize. Golden Globe nominations can shape the momentum of awards season, making the category choice more than a technicality for a genre already facing an uphill campaign.

content.headline: James Dean was more than the rebel: the vulnerable actor behind the image
content.shortHeadline: James Dean beyond the rebel image
content.standfirst: A new account of East of Eden’s production revisits Dean’s restless, vulnerable performance and the fame that frightened him. The film, the review argues, is most affecting when it shows not a pin-up rebel but a son desperate for his father’s acceptance.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.title: A raw performance in East of Eden
segments.body: Elia Kazan channelled Dean’s complicated feelings about his father into the role of Cal Trask. The account revisits a set moment in which Dean’s improvised outburst provoked a real reaction from co-star Raymond Massey. The resulting performance is restless and awkward, but the review argues that those qualities make Cal someone viewers cling to rather than simply admire.

segments.title: Fame, myth and a human moment
segments.body: Dean died at 24, after three starring roles, and his death intensified the public image of him as an icon of living fast and dying young. The review finds a different kind of power in East of Eden’s scene of Cal embracing his father after a rejected gift: a desperate, vulnerable boy reaching for someone who cannot return the gesture.

content.headline: Sense and Sensibility finds new force in Austen’s divided sisters
content.shortHeadline: A new Sense and Sensibility puts Austen’s sisters in focus
content.standfirst: Georgia Oakley’s darker adaptation follows Elinor and Marianne through financial precarity, grief and competing ideas about love. The review sees the novel’s tension between restraint and feeling as a modern dilemma, though finds the film uneven.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility

segments.title: Two sisters, two ways to cope
segments.body: Daisy Edgar-Jones plays the guarded Elinor and Esmé Creed-Miles the romantic Marianne, whose family’s loss of fortune makes marriage a matter of security as well as affection. The review argues that their contrast still speaks to contemporary pressure to balance privacy and self-expression, and financial uncertainty with the desire to live passionately.

segments.title: An adaptation with a modern echo
segments.body: The film stays largely within its period setting, while a darker tone and occasional modern touches frame Marianne’s relationship with Willoughby as a familiar pattern of charm, implication and withdrawal. The reviewer finds the film hit and miss, but says Austen’s question—whether to follow heart or head—still resonates beyond the romance plot.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after the Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces a break after its Disney+ deal ends
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ collaboration, cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking a new funding partner. Fans and former contributors disagree about why the show faltered, but the next Doctor and the series’ future remain unknown.

image.caption: Several of Doctor Who’s modern incarnations, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.title: A pause without a Doctor
segments.body: Since the 2025 series ended with Ncuti Gatwa’s departure, Doctor Who has been off air. The BBC has ended its partnership with Disney+, put the series out for competitive tender and cancelled a planned Christmas special. The corporation has declined to comment further, and no new Doctor has been announced.

segments.title: What went wrong—and what should return
segments.body: The piece canvasses competing explanations, including scripts that some viewers found confusing, the changing showrunner and the end of Disney+ funding. Lifelong fan Frank Skinner says the programme did not need billions to tell a good story; scriptwriter Nina Metivier points to its core values of kindness and curiosity. Both he and TV historian Matthew Sweet expect it to return, but want it back on screen.

content.headline: Mike Flanagan’s Carrie adaptation revives debate about casting and change
content.shortHeadline: Why Mike Flanagan’s Carrie is already stirring debate
content.standfirst: Fans have questioned whether the new series captures Stephen King’s angry, physically “plain” heroine. A horror scholar and film-maker argue that the adaptation changes key details but may still work on its own terms.

image.caption: A promotional still from the new Carrie series.

sources.originalTitle: Why a new TV version of horror classic Carrie is already annoying people

segments.title: A different Carrie White
segments.body: Online criticism has focused on casting and on screen versions that soften Carrie compared with King’s novel. Flanagan’s series makes her newly home-schooled and “untraumatised” when she arrives at school, a change that makes the bullying feel newly cruel. The BBC feature notes that the show also brings social media into the story of teenage humiliation.

segments.title: Faithfulness versus reinvention
segments.body: Horror scholar Sorcha Ní Fhlainn argues that the series gives Carrie’s otherness a different form, through her homemade clothes and home-schooling. Film-maker Liam Gavin says adaptations can face market pressures in casting, but also cautions against expecting directors to follow a source text slavishly. The article’s verdict is that the series is a layered story for the present, even if debate over its choices continues.

perspectives.body: The article presents two distinct considerations: a commercial casting system may favour conventionally attractive leads, while creative departures can also be a deliberate adaptation choice. It does not treat fidelity to King’s description as the only measure of success.

content.headline: War turns a rich couple’s divorce into glossy legal melodrama
content.shortHeadline: War makes a high-stakes divorce a gleeful TV spectacle
content.standfirst: Sienna Miller and Dominic West lead George Kay’s drama about a public divorce, money and duelling legal teams. The Guardian review enjoys its extravagant plotting as a welcome escape from the news.

image.caption: Sienna Miller, James McArdle and Phoebe Fox in War.

sources.originalTitle: War review – Sienna Miller and Dominic West’s hellish divorce drama is massive, massive fun

segments.title: Money, marriage and manoeuvring
segments.body: West plays a social-media mogul and Miller his film-star wife, who seeks leverage as their marriage breaks down. Their divorce brings two rival law firms into a web of tactical moves, media attention and personal vendettas. The review relishes the series’ twists and lavish setting rather than asking viewers to invest in its characters’ virtue.

segments.title: An unapologetic palate-cleanser
segments.body: The review calls War high-quality balderdash: a fast-moving, high-stakes soap opera powered by money, class conflict, sex and elaborate legal manoeuvres. It praises performances across the ensemble, including Pip Torrens as the scheming St John Smallwood, and sees the show’s excess as part of its appeal.

content.headline: Get Jiro turns restaurant culture into a bloody turf war
content.shortHeadline: Get Jiro serves food satire with a side of ultraviolence
content.standfirst: Anthony Bourdain’s graphic novel becomes an adult animation about a sushi chef navigating a violent Los Angeles restaurant war. The Guardian finds the food satire gleefully excessive, with class politics simmering beneath the gore.

image.caption: Sushi chef Jiro in Get Jiro.

sources.originalTitle: Get Jiro: Anthony Bourdain’s ultraviolent sushi chef makes for wild, pulpy television

segments.title: Chefs rule a lawless Los Angeles
segments.body: In a near-future city where most pleasures are virtual, food remains a powerful physical experience—and chefs have become crime-lord figures. Jiro is a taciturn sushi master who is no stranger to violence. The series pushes its premise into grotesque comedy, with fights involving knives, cheese graters and even custard.

segments.title: A satire with bite
segments.body: The review enjoys the collision between refined food language and cartoon brutality, but says the show is not for the squeamish. Based on a graphic novel co-written by Bourdain, it also treats food as a marker of class and power, beneath the pulp action and elaborate dishes.

content.headline: Lenny Rush brings comic awkwardness and pathos to The Reluctant Vampire
content.shortHeadline: Lenny Rush on finding belonging in The Reluctant Vampire
content.standfirst: The 17-year-old actor leads a comedy adapted from Eric Morecambe’s children’s book, playing a young vampire who discovers he is human. Rush talks about the show’s all-ages humour, his own visibility and the risk of being pigeonholed.

image.caption: Lenny Rush as Val in The Reluctant Vampire.

sources.originalTitle: Fangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedy

segments.title: A vampire who doesn’t fit in
segments.body: Val comes from a family of vampires but lacks their skills: he has no sharp teeth and hates blood. Rush says the character’s attempts to belong at school make the story relatable beyond its supernatural premise. The series pairs slapstick with pathos, drawing on a comic tradition that takes absurd situations seriously.

segments.title: Growing up on screen
segments.body: Rush says he was surprised by messages from parents whose children with dwarfism felt more confident after seeing him on television. He did not begin acting to become a spokesperson, and says he hopes not to be confined to comic roles. He also credits his parents for keeping school and friendships in view while he worked from a young age.

content.headline: The Split Up puts a British Asian family at the centre of a divorce drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up brings a new British Asian family to the drama
content.standfirst: The Manchester-set spin-off keeps the original series’ high-stakes divorce cases but follows a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Its creators describe representation through the ordinary, complicated life of one family.

image.caption: Ritu Arya and Abi Morgan, whose original series The Split inspired the spin-off.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.title: A new family in the same world
segments.body: Ritu Arya plays Aria Kishan, a barrister expecting to take over her father’s firm until family loss and a former love unsettle her plans. The six-part drama continues The Split’s mix of legal cases and private turmoil, but moves the story from London to Manchester and centres a new family.

segments.title: Representation through everyday life
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted British Asian characters living ordinary lives, rather than being defined by the exceptional circumstances often assigned to them on screen. Original series creator Abi Morgan has stepped back from writing, acting as a supporter of the new creative team. Morgan also sees the show’s ensemble of women working across production as part of a broader effort to build opportunity.

content.headline: Nigella Lawson gives Bake Off a new appetite for pleasure
content.shortHeadline: Nigella Lawson brings unapologetic pleasure to Bake Off
content.standfirst: The new judge’s delight in eating has changed the tone of The Great British Bake Off for these reviewers. One sees a welcome challenge to food shame and skinny culture; another says her glamour rescues a familiar format from staleness.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson, the new judge on The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Nigella is dismantling skinny culture one ‘naughty cookie’ at a time
Nigella’s glamour saves Bake Off’s stale mix

segments.title: Pleasure without apology
segments.body: One review focuses on Lawson’s refusal to call food “naughty” and her unapologetic enjoyment of contestants’ baking. Against a culture saturated with weight-loss messaging, the writer sees that pleasure as quietly radical, particularly on a mainstream show watched outside Lawson’s own cooking programmes.

segments.title: A familiar tent, refreshed
segments.body: A second review finds the new judge a shrewd addition to a show that rarely changes. Lawson brings confidence and sensuality to the tent, it says, even as the first episode retains familiar challenges, jokes and mishaps. Both reviews see her as a source of renewed energy, though they emphasise different reasons.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s episode review stresses Lawson’s natural glamour and the show’s unchanging comfort-watch formula, arguing that she makes the programme “the same but better”. It focuses on the episode’s challenges and contestants rather than the wider body-image argument.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors opens with Richard E Grant’s astonishing confession
content.shortHeadline: Richard E Grant’s confession gives The Celebrity Traitors a wild start
content.standfirst: Grant immediately told fellow contestants he was a Traitor, throwing the new series into chaos. Three reviews relish the blunder for different reasons, while overnight figures show 8.9 million people watched the opener.

image.caption: Richard E Grant and Maya Jama, the first two Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Richard E Grant has one hope of lasting on Celebrity Traitors: leaning into his eccentricity
The Celebrity Traitors review – Ross Kemp really needs to get a grip
Richard E Grant has already ruined The Celebrity Traitors. It’s brilliant
Celebrity Traitors debut draws almost 9m viewers and more than half of TV audience

segments.title: A game changed by one admission
segments.body: After being selected as a Traitor, Grant told Joe Lycett the truth when asked. The reviews describe a stunned cast and a scramble to explain the confession away: some contestants treat it as a joke, while Grant and fellow Traitor Maya Jama have to manage the suspicion it creates. The episode ends before the first banishment is shown.

segments.title: An unpredictable format draws a big audience
segments.body: The Guardian’s commentary asks whether Grant’s eccentricity can help him survive; the i Paper calls the mistake a spectacular start that may define the series. The opener averaged 8.9 million viewers, according to overnight data cited by the Guardian, up from 6.1 million for the previous series debut. The same report says it reached 83.5% of 16-to-34-year-olds watching television in that slot.

perspectives.body: The i Paper argues that a celebrity cast makes the format more revealing because viewers arrive with expectations of the contestants. It sees Grant’s mistake not only as a blunder but as the kind of unpredictable behaviour that can make the game feel fresh.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has excellent combat but little else to sustain it
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day’s great combat can’t save its repetition
content.standfirst: The prequel captures the series’ visceral cover-based fighting, but its repetitive routes, cluttered collectibles and limited variety leave the Guardian reviewer bored by an alien invasion that should feel urgent.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.title: The series at its best—and then again
segments.body: E-Day returns to the moment aliens emerge from the ground, putting Marcus Fenix and his squad amid the chaos. Its opening hours revive the horror and tactical combat of the early games, but the campaign repeatedly sends players through the same areas, with few meaningful changes to break up the fighting.

segments.title: Excellent mechanics, frustrating exploration
segments.body: The review praises more fluid movement, weighty weapons and destructible environments, calling this the best the series’ combat has felt. But large areas are packed with collectibles, while the game can punish players for exploring beyond its intended route. The result, the reviewer argues, is a safe experience that spends its strongest ideas early.

content.headline: Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil recreates the fear of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: Resident Evil works by making viewers feel like players
content.standfirst: Rather than relying on familiar heroes, Cregger’s film follows an ordinary courier through a world of scarce ammunition, strange encounters and escalating body horror. The Guardian argues that it adapts the experience of playing Resident Evil, not just its lore.

image.caption: Director Zach Cregger and actor Austin Abrams on the Resident Evil set.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.title: A player’s journey on screen
segments.body: The film’s courier, Bryan, enters a viral outbreak without weapons or a clear understanding of what is happening. He moves through familiar kinds of locations—from an abandoned farmhouse to a hospital and sewer—finding stronger weapons but never enough ammunition. Brief encounters and found recordings provide information while keeping danger close.

segments.title: Adapting a game’s structure
segments.body: The review argues that the film’s fidelity lies less in including established heroes such as Leon or Claire than in recreating the player’s uncertainty. It compares the approach with films that explore video-game mechanics themselves: audiences must learn the world’s rules as they follow a vulnerable character through it.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 delivers the aerial thrills of a Top Gun fantasy
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 makes flight combat thrilling and cinematic
content.standfirst: The latest Ace Combat pairs spectacular dogfights with a more expressive story and accessible flight controls. Its reviewer praises the aerial action and presentation, while noting that battle clutter and brief multiplayer access leave some questions.

image.caption: A fighter jet cuts through the skies in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.title: The thrill of the dogfight
segments.body: Ace Combat 8 delivers the series’ familiar rush: clouds part, missiles lock on and fighter jets weave through dense fire. Missions vary from bombing runs and escorts to hunting invisible aircraft and attacking a land battleship. Beginners can use simplified controls, while experienced players can opt for more demanding manoeuvres.

segments.title: A bigger cinematic frame
segments.body: The game adds environmental destruction and more fully animated first-person sequences, giving wing-mates and combat moments greater emotional presence. The review says the story borrows from Top Gun: Maverick and can stumble over exposition, but finds the cinematography, music and voice acting unexpectedly affecting. The reviewer could not properly try its online multiplayer mode.

content.headline: Roblox phishing scams use fake free-Robux offers to target children
content.shortHeadline: How fake free-Robux offers steal children’s Roblox logins
content.standfirst: Fraudsters use convincing login pages to collect children’s passwords and authentication codes, then steal in-game currency or personal data. Security specialists advise opening Roblox directly rather than following links in videos or chats.

image.caption: Roblox advises users to avoid links from unknown senders or websites.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children

segments.title: A familiar-looking trap
segments.body: Scammers promise free Robux through links shared in YouTube or TikTok comments and Discord chats. The link opens a fake login page designed to look like Roblox, which may then redirect the child to the real service. The false offer can be hard to spot, and the criminal may already have the account details.

segments.title: Practical steps—and uncertain recovery
segments.body: NordVPN specialists advise children to open Roblox through its official app or website and never share passwords, two-factor codes or backup codes. Roblox says it has security measures to limit account theft, but does not guarantee it can restore compromised accounts or recover lost currency except in very limited circumstances.

content.headline: Replaying Call of Duty with his son brings a father back to gaming
content.shortHeadline: A father and son revisit the game that started their bond
content.standfirst: After nearly two decades, a father and his 22-year-old son return to the Call of Duty missions they first played together. Their teamwork turns a once-unfinished challenge into a moving reminder of how gaming can make time together.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game a father and son played together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.title: A mission 17 years in the making
segments.body: The pair return to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2’s co-op missions, which they first attempted when the son was five. Their styles clash—one moves cautiously, the other charges ahead—until they learn to divide tasks and take out the guard dogs first. They finally complete a mission they had failed for years.

segments.title: Play as time together
segments.body: The writer describes the sessions as a rare return to carefree gaming, before work and family responsibilities made free hours harder to find. The son says he will remember the time as some of their best together. They expect to move to different parts of the world in a few months, making the shared play feel especially precious.

content.headline: The volunteer Pokémon professors who keep tournaments running
content.shortHeadline: Meet the volunteer judges behind Pokémon’s competitive scene
content.standfirst: At the 2026 world championships, volunteer professors judged matches, helped players and kept events safe. Their work is largely behind the scenes, and the Pokémon Company declined to give an official account of how they are compensated.

image.caption: Attendees at the 2026 Pokémon World Championships in San Francisco.

sources.originalTitle: Meet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling

segments.title: More than referees
segments.body: Around 300 Pokémon professors were present at the world championships in San Francisco, according to a Pokémon Company International representative. Their roles range from technical support to judging card games, recording results and making sure competitors understand the rules. Several interviewed volunteers said they worked their way up through local events.

segments.title: Rules, care and compensation
segments.body: Head judge Gemma Byard says professors must manage disputes as well as rules, while Evelyne de Groot describes the work as a form of customer service that helps players enjoy the event. Most interviewees declined to discuss compensation. One said some European volunteers receive merchandise, while US regional staff are paid; the company declined an official comment on payment.

content.headline: Why players are pushing back against games that hold their hands
content.shortHeadline: Players want games to leave room for discovery
content.standfirst: Viral criticism of Marvel’s Wolverine has renewed debate about highlighted routes, constant prompts and automated play. The Guardian argues that good game design needs enough friction for agency and learning, not just difficulty for its own sake.

image.caption: Marvel’s Wolverine, whose guidance prompts have drawn player criticism.

sources.originalTitle: Why fans are digging their claws into Wolverine over its patronising gameplay

segments.title: Help that becomes overbearing
segments.body: Clips from Wolverine show objectives marked by visual cues, trails and repeated prompts, prompting players to mock how little the game leaves them to discover. The piece places this in a wider trend of blockbuster games making routes and tasks increasingly explicit, while stressing that the criticism is about design that removes agency—not about rejecting help for every player.

segments.title: Difficulty is not the same as friction
segments.body: The writer distinguishes difficulty, which can result from controls or balance, from friction: the intentional distance between a player and a goal. Games can use that space to invite strategy, practice and discovery. Examples such as Hollow Knight: Silksong and Blue Prince show how demanding combat and unclear objectives can each ask players to participate in different ways.

segments.title: A question for big-budget design
segments.body: The article argues that at its worst, constant guidance removes the challenge that makes play satisfying. It contrasts that approach with games that trust players to learn a world and its rules, and hopes the reaction to Wolverine will remind publishers that participation—not just smooth progress—is part of the appeal.

content.headline: Could romancing a video-game character count as cheating?
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s virtual romance has revived the cheating debate
content.standfirst: Some social-media users argue that maintaining a relationship with GTA VI characters Lucia or Jason crosses a line. The Guardian sees the reaction as less about a game’s mechanics than about loneliness, unmet needs and differing relationship boundaries.

image.caption: GTA VI protagonists Lucia and Jason.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.title: A game romance sparks an online argument
segments.body: The game’s protagonists, Lucia and Jason, can strengthen their relationship through dates, messages and other interactions. Some TikTok users have called that “micro-cheating”, while the article notes that the mechanic works both ways: players can invest in either character. Dating mechanics have appeared in games for decades, but GTA VI’s reach may bring them to new audiences.

segments.title: The concern beneath the joke
segments.body: The writer rejects the idea that in-game romance is inherently unfaithful, while acknowledging that couples set different boundaries. She argues that frustration may come from seeing a partner invest attention in a fictional relationship while neglecting a real one. Sex educator Dee Whitnell similarly says feeling underappreciated can make that contrast painful; the article links the debate to wider anxieties about loneliness and dating.
